preamble: Fronting of the close central unrounded vowel [ɨ] to [i], usually as a merger of the two vowels. Old Czech of the 13th century still kept y [ɨ] (from Proto-Slavic *y) apart from i; after the loss of consonant palatalization the two were pronounced alike by the 15th century, and Czech spelling now keeps y and i only as an etymological distinction. Proto-Slavic *y likewise became i in the South Slavic area, as the Croatian recension of Church Slavonic shows (byti > biti 'to be').

examples.note: Modern Czech syn [ˈsɪn] has a later lax short vowel.
Long ý also gave a diphthong /aj/ (Common Czech ej); Wiktionary lists 15th-century /ˈdiːm/ and /ˈdajm/.

sources: Wikipedia contributors (2026). History of the Czech language. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Czech_language
